title: Dynamic Programming
summary: Comprehensive Dynamic Programming module that covers from the theoretical foundations (requirements, structures and recursive modeling) to the advanced implementation of classic problems such as Fibonacci and LCS. Includes detailed comparison of Top-Down vs Bottom-Up approaches, solution reconstruction using path tables, and common 1D/2D modeling patterns.

terms.label: Dynamic Programming
terms.definition: Design technique that solves subproblems only once, saves its results, and reuses them to construct the solution to the original problem.

terms.label: Optimal substructure
terms.definition: Property by which an optimal solution to the large problem can be constructed from optimal solutions of subproblems.

terms.label: Optimality principle
terms.definition: Condition that requires that global optimal decisions are compatible with optimal decisions in the subproblems.

terms.label: Overlapping subproblems
terms.definition: Situation where recursion requests the same subproblems several times.

terms.label: Recursive model
terms.definition: Mathematical definition of the problem through base cases and general cases. It is the starting point before designing the solution with PD.

terms.label: PD model
terms.definition: Tabulated or memoized version of the recursive model, where each state is stored in a data structure.

terms.label: Status
terms.definition: Minimum set of parameters that identifies a subproblem within Dynamic Programming.

terms.label: Optimum table
terms.definition: Table that stores the best calculated value for each subproblem.

terms.label: Path table
terms.definition: Table that stores the decision or provenance that produced the optimum for each subproblem.

terms.label: Vector SOA
terms.definition: Final sequence of decisions reconstructed by going backwards through the path table.

terms.label: Memoization
terms.definition: Top-Down approach that preserves the recursive structure, but saves each solved subproblem so as not to recalculate it.

terms.label: Tabulation
terms.definition: Bottom-Up approach that fills a table from the base cases to the final problem.

terms.label: Top-Down
terms.definition: Implementation with recursion and memoization. Subproblems are calculated on demand.

terms.label: Bottom-Up
terms.definition: Iterative implementation that computes small subproblems first and then larger ones.

terms.label: LCS
terms.definition: Longest Common Subsequence. Problem that searches for the longest subsequence common to two strings, preserving order but without requiring consecutiveness.

terms.label: Subsequence
terms.definition: Sequence obtained by eliminating zero or more elements from another sequence, without changing the relative order of the remaining elements.

terms.label: dp[i][j]
terms.definition: Cell that stores the optimal value of a subproblem identified by the prefixes X[1..i] and Y[1..j].

terms.label: Backward tour
terms.definition: Reconstruction process that starts from the final cell of the table and follows the saved decisions until reaching a base case.

terms.label: Diagonal in LCS
terms.definition: Reconstruction move used when characters match. Indicates that that character belongs to an LCS.

terms.label: Up in LCS
terms.definition: Move that discards a character from X and goes from dp[i][j] to dp[i-1][j].

terms.label: Left in LCS
terms.definition: Move that discards a character from Y and goes from dp[i][j] to dp[i][j-1].

terms.label: Spatial optimization
terms.definition: Reducing the space used by a PD table when the calculation of a row or cell only depends on a limited number of previous rows or states.

chapters.title: Dynamic Programming — Part 1
chapters.summary: Fundamentals of Dynamic Programming: requirements, structures, recursive modeling, translation to PD, Factorial and Fibonacci.

learningObjectives.text: Understand Dynamic Programming as a technique to eliminate recalculation through memory.
Differentiate Dynamic Programming from Divide and Conquer.

content.text: Dynamic Programming is an algorithmic design technique that takes a recursively defined problem, detects that some subproblems are repeated, and avoids solving them more than once by saving its answers.
Naive recursion asks the same thing many times. Dynamic Programming responds once, saves the response, and reuses that result when you need it again.
The main trade-off is clear: PD usually reduces time, but increases space. That space appears in tables, dictionaries, matrices or vectors that store partial results.

blocks.title: Not every recursive algorithm needs PD

content.text: If the subproblems are not repeated, saving results does not contribute much. PD is not synonymous with optimized recursion; it is recursion or tabulation with real reuse of subproblems.

learningObjectives.text: Compare the implementation differences between Top-Down and Bottom-Up.

content.text: Top-Down and Bottom-Up solve the same Dynamic Programming model, but they go through the states in a different way. Top-Down preserves recursion and computes on demand. Bottom-Up eliminates recursion and fills the table in an explicit order.

cells.text: Recursive. Modifies the original recursive by adding memory.
Iterative. Use cycles to fill tables.

It is usually regular: rows, columns, diagonals or increasing lengths.
Same asymptotic order on the effectively resolved states.
Same asymptotic order if the same states are filled.
Memoization table or dictionary plus recursive stack.
Worse: entering and exiting each recursive environment is difficult.
Useful when the pattern of states is irregular.
Preferable when the filling pattern is regular.

content.text: If you can identify a clear order of filling the table, use Bottom-Up. If you can't because states depend on input or appear irregularly, use Top-Down. It is not an aesthetic decision: it is a decision of dependencies.

blocks.title: Decision between Top-Down and Bottom-Up
Same order does not mean same real time

content.text: Two versions can have the same asymptotic order and still have different real times. Bottom-Up usually has better constants because it avoids the fixed cost of creating and destroying recursive environments.
